method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from ONE source: the pertussis chapter of the Australian Immunisation Handbook, retrieved 2026-09-23 and quoted verbatim. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable against the retrieved file. ⚠️ LICENCE: the Handbook is FREE TO READ but is NOT openly licensed -- health.gov.au states 'all other rights are reserved'. It is quoted with full attribution on the same footing this compendium already uses for the Stroke Foundation, Kidney Health Australia and NHFA/CSANZ, none of which are CC BY either. ⚠️ SCOPE IS PREVENTION, NOT TREATMENT: the Handbook gives no antibiotic, dose or duration for pertussis, and names the CDNA national guidelines for that, which were NOT retrieved.

claims.claim: CHILDHOOD SCHEDULE: pertussis-containing vaccine is recommended in a 5-DOSE SCHEDULE AT 2, 4, 6 AND 18 MONTHS, AND 4 YEARS OF AGE. ⚠️ INFANTS CAN HAVE THEIR 1ST DOSE AS EARLY AS 6 WEEKS OF AGE, and if given at 6 weeks they SHOULD STILL RECEIVE THEIR NEXT SCHEDULED DOSES AT 4 MONTHS AND 6 MONTHS
claims.source_text: Pertussis-containing vaccine is recommended in a 5-dose schedule at 2, 4, 6 and 18 months, and 4 years of age. … Infants can have their 1st dose of pertussis-containing vaccine as early as 6 weeks of age. … If the 1st dose of pertussis-containing vaccine is given at the age of 6 weeks, infants should still receive their next scheduled doses at 4 months and 6 months of age.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ THE 18-MONTH AND 4-YEAR DOSES ARE NEEDED BECAUSE PERTUSSIS IMMUNITY WANES AFTER THE INFANT DOSES, and PRESCHOOL AND SCHOOL-AGED CHILDREN CAN BE AN IMPORTANT SOURCE OF INFECTION FOR INFANTS
claims.source_text: Doses of pertussis-containing vaccine at 18 months and 4 years of age are needed because pertussis immunity wanes after receiving the infant doses. … Preschool and school-aged children can be an important source of infection for infants.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: VACCINES USED AT EACH SCHEDULE POINT: at 2, 4 and 6 months DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib; at 18 months DTPa; at 4 years DTPa-IPV. ⚠️ THERE IS NO PREFERENTIAL RECOMMENDATION between DT5aP-hepB-IPV-Hib(PRP-OMP) (Vaxelis) and DT3aP-hepB-IPV-Hib(PRP-TT) (Infanrix hexa)
claims.source_text: 2, 4 and 6 months of age — DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib … 18 months of age — DTPa … 4 years of age — DTPa-IPV … There is no preferential recommendation between the use of DT5aP-hepB-IPV-Hib(PRP-OMP) vaccine (Vaxelis) and DT3aP-hepB-IPV-Hib(PRP-TT) vaccine (Infanrix hexa)
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ADOLESCENTS aged 11-13 years are recommended a BOOSTER using the REDUCED ANTIGEN dTpa VACCINE. ⚠️ THE OPTIMAL AGE IS 11-13 YEARS, adolescents need it BECAUSE IMMUNITY WANES AFTER THE CHILDHOOD DOSE AT 4 YEARS, and they are recommended 1 DOSE REGARDLESS OF THE NUMBER OF PREVIOUS DOSES
claims.source_text: A booster dose of pertussis-containing vaccine is recommended for adolescents, using the reduced antigen dTpa vaccine. The optimal age for administering this dose is 11–13 years. … Adolescents need a booster dose because pertussis immunity wanes after the childhood dose at 4 years of age. … Adolescents are recommended to receive 1 dose of pertussis-containing vaccine, regardless of the number of previous doses
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ PREGNANCY — dTpa AS A SINGLE DOSE IN EACH PREGNANCY. VACCINATION DURING PREGNANCY REDUCES THE RISK OF PERTUSSIS IN YOUNG INFANTS AGED 3-4 MONTHS BY 90%, by transplacental transfer of antibodies. It is recommended in EACH pregnancy INCLUDING CLOSELY SPACED ONES, because antibody levels WANE OVER TIME and THE LEVEL NEEDED IN MOTHERS TO PASS ON IMMUNITY IS UNKNOWN
claims.source_text: dTpa vaccine is recommended as a single dose in each pregnancy. … Vaccination during pregnancy reduces the risk of pertussis in young infants (aged 3-4 months) by 90%. … This results from direct passive protection by transplacental transfer of pertussis antibodies from the mother to the fetus during pregnancy. … Vaccination is recommended during each pregnancy, including pregnancies that are closely spaced, to provide maximal protection to every infant. … vaccine-induced pertussis antibody levels wane over time the antibody level needed in mothers to pass on immunity to newborn infants is unknown
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ THE OPTIMAL TIME FOR PERTUSSIS VACCINATION IN PREGNANCY IS BETWEEN 20 AND 32 WEEKS GESTATION. The stated reasons: protective antibody levels are detected in infants born to mothers vaccinated in that window; MATERNAL ANTIBODIES ARE ACTIVELY TRANSPORTED TO THE FETUS FROM 13 WEEKS, WITH MAXIMUM TRANSFER FROM 30 WEEKS; and ⚠️ PERTUSSIS ANTIBODY LEVELS DO NOT PEAK UNTIL ABOUT 2 WEEKS AFTER VACCINATION
claims.source_text: The optimal time for pertussis vaccination in pregnancy is between 20 and 32 weeks gestation. … levels of pertussis antibodies that are likely to be protective are detected in infants born to mothers vaccinated between 20 and 32 weeks gestation maternal antibodies are actively transported to the fetus from 13 weeks, … with maximum transfer 30 weeks gestation onwards … pertussis antibody levels do not peak until about 2 weeks after vaccination
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ ADULT HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS AND CARERS of infants under 6 months are recommended dTpa AT LEAST 2 WEEKS BEFORE THEY HAVE CLOSE CONTACT WITH THE INFANT, if their last dose was MORE THAN 10 YEARS AGO. Pertussis in infants under 6 months is associated with SIGNIFICANT MORBIDITY
claims.source_text: Adult household contacts and carers of infants <6 months of age are recommended to receive dTpa vaccine at least 2 weeks before they have close contact with the infant if their last dose was more than 10 years ago. … Pertussis infection in infants <6 months of age is associated with significant morbidity.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ADULTS AGED 65 YEARS AND OVER are recommended a dTpa dose IF THEY HAVE NOT HAD ONE IN THE PAST 10 YEARS, because pertussis is ASSOCIATED WITH INCREASED MORBIDITY IN OLDER PEOPLE and because of WANING OF VACCINE IMMUNITY
claims.source_text: Adults aged ≥65 years are recommended to receive a dTpa dose if they have not had one in the past 10 years. … This is because pertussis is associated with increased morbidity in older people
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: TRANSMISSION AND NATURAL HISTORY: pertussis is a RESPIRATORY INFECTION THAT SPREADS BY AEROSOLS, with an INCUBATION PERIOD OF 7-20 DAYS. It is HIGHLY INFECTIOUS IN UNVACCINATED PEOPLE AND CAN INFECT 90% OF SUSCEPTIBLE HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS. ⚠️ NATURAL INFECTION DOES NOT PROVIDE LONG-TERM PROTECTION AND REPEAT INFECTION CAN OCCUR
claims.source_text: Pertussis is a respiratory infection that spreads by aerosols. It has an incubation period of 7–20 days. It is highly infectious in unvaccinated people, and can infect 90% of susceptible household contacts. … Natural infection does not provide long-term protection. Repeat infection can occur.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ CLINICAL FEATURES — THE CHARACTERISTIC WHOOP IS THE EXCEPTION, NOT THE RULE. Unvaccinated children can have a paroxysmal cough with a whoop, but THIS IS LESS COMMON IN PEOPLE WITH IMMUNITY FROM VACCINATION OR INFECTION. ⚠️ IN VERY YOUNG INFANTS THE COUGH MAY BE MINIMAL OR ABSENT, AND THE ONLY SYMPTOMS MAY BE APNOEA OR CYANOSIS
claims.source_text: Unvaccinated children can have a characteristic paroxysmal cough with a ‘whoop’ when breathing in. This is less common in people who have immunity as a result of vaccination or infection . … In very young infants, the cough may be minimal or absent, and the only symptoms may be apnoea or cyanosis.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ THE CASE FOR A LOW THRESHOLD TO TEST: EACH YEAR MORE THAN 25% OF ADULTS HAVE A COUGH THAT LASTS AT LEAST 5 DAYS, AND BORDETELLA PERTUSSIS MAY CAUSE UP TO 7% OF THESE ILLNESSES. Patients and physicians MAY NOT BE AWARE OF THE DISEASE, AND DIAGNOSTIC TESTS SOMETIMES HAVE LIMITED SENSITIVITY
claims.source_text: Each year, more than 25% of adults have a cough that lasts at least 5 days. Bordetella pertussis may cause up to 7% of these illnesses. … Patients and physicians may not be aware of the disease, and diagnostic tests sometimes have limited sensitivity.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: DIAGNOSIS: confirmed by CULTURE OR NUCLEIC ACID TESTING of a nasal or throat swab or nasopharyngeal aspirate, OR SEROLOGY. The appropriate test DEPENDS ON AGE, VACCINATION HISTORY AND DURATION OF SYMPTOMS, and NUCLEIC ACID TESTING IS USUALLY THE DIAGNOSTIC METHOD OF CHOICE
claims.source_text: culture or nucleic acid testing of a nasal or throat swab, or nasopharyngeal aspirate specimen, or serology The appropriate diagnostic test depends on age, vaccination history and duration of symptoms. Nucleic acid testing is usually the diagnostic method of choice.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ EPIDEMIOLOGY — WHO INFECTS INFANTS. NOTIFICATION RATES ARE HIGHER AMONG ABORIGINAL AND TORRES STRAIT ISLANDER CHILDREN COMPARED TO NON-INDIGENOUS CHILDREN ACROSS ALL AGE GROUPS UNDER 5. In highly immunised communities pertussis occurs in ADULTS AND ADOLESCENTS through waning immunity and THESE PEOPLE ARE A SIGNIFICANT RESERVOIR OF INFECTION. ⚠️ HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS AND CARERS ARE OFTEN THE SOURCE OF INFECTION IN INFANTS, AND PARENTS ARE THE SOURCE IN MORE THAN 50% OF CASES
claims.source_text: Notification rates are higher among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children compared to non-Indigenous children across all age groups <5 years. … In highly immunised communities, pertussis can occur in adults and adolescents as a result of waning immunity. … These people are a significant reservoir of infection . … Household contacts and carers are often the source of infection in infants. Parents are the source in more than 50% of cases.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ PUBLIC HEALTH: PERTUSSIS, BOTH SUSPECTED AND CONFIRMED, IS A NOTIFIABLE DISEASE IN ALL STATES AND TERRITORIES IN AUSTRALIA. SUSPECTED CASES SHOULD BE INVESTIGATED REGARDLESS OF VACCINATION STATUS, BECAUSE IMMUNISATION IS NOT 100% EFFECTIVE AND IMMUNITY WANES OVER TIME. People with suspected infection SHOULD RECEIVE APPROPRIATE ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY IF CORYZA STARTED LESS THAN 21 DAYS AGO
claims.source_text: Pertussis (both suspected and confirmed) is a notifiable disease in all states and territories in Australia. … Suspected cases of pertussis should be investigated, regardless of vaccination status. This is because immunisation is not 100% effective and immunity wanes over time. … People with suspected pertussis infection should receive appropriate antibiotic therapy if coryza started less than 21 days ago.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ CONTRAINDICATIONS — THE ONLY ABSOLUTE ONES ARE ANAPHYLAXIS AFTER A PREVIOUS DOSE OF ANY ACELLULAR PERTUSSIS-CONTAINING VACCINE, OR ANAPHYLAXIS AFTER ANY COMPONENT OF ONE. PRECAUTION: the product information for Adacel states THE TIP CAP OF THE SYRINGE CONTAINS LATEX — consider an alternative product in people with latex allergy or sensitivity
claims.source_text: The only absolute contraindications to acellular pertussis–containing vaccines are: anaphylaxis after a previous dose of any acellular pertussis–containing vaccine anaphylaxis after any component of an acellular pertussis–containing vaccine … The product information for Adacel states that the tip cap of the syringe contains latex. Consider using an alternative product in people with an allergy or sensitivity to latex.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ADVERSE EVENTS: acellular pertussis-containing vaccines are associated with a LOWER INCIDENCE OF FEVER (APPROXIMATELY 20%) THAN WHOLE-CELL VACCINES (APPROXIMATELY 45%), and a LOWER INCIDENCE OF LOCAL ADVERSE EVENTS (APPROXIMATELY 10%) THAN WHOLE-CELL (APPROXIMATELY 40%). ⚠️ WHOLE-CELL PERTUSSIS VACCINES ARE NO LONGER AVAILABLE IN AUSTRALIA. EXTENSIVE LIMB SWELLING OCCURS IN UNDER 2% OF CHILDREN AFTER BOOSTER DOSES OF DTPa, defined as swelling and/or redness involving at least half the circumference of the limb and the joints both above and below the injection site
claims.source_text: Acellular pertussis–containing vaccines are associated with a lower incidence of fever (approximately 20%) than whole-cell pertussis–containing vaccines (approximately 45%). … Acellular pertussis–containing vaccines are also associated with a lower incidence of local adverse events (approximately 10%) than whole-cell pertussis–containing vaccines (approximately 40%). … Whole-cell pertussis-containing vaccines are no longer available in Australia. … Extensive limb swelling occurs in <2% of children after booster doses of DTPa . … at least half the circumference of the limb the joints both above and below the injection site
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: dTpa VACCINE COMPOSITION, from the product entry for Adacel: each 0.5 mL MONODOSE VIAL OR PRE-FILLED SYRINGE contains AT LEAST 2 IU DIPHTHERIA TOXOID, AT LEAST 20 IU TETANUS TOXOID, 2.5 microgram PERTUSSIS TOXOID, 5 microgram FILAMENTOUS HAEMAGGLUTININ, 3 microgram PERTACTIN and 5 microgram PERTUSSIS FIMBRIAE TYPES 2 AND 3, adsorbed on aluminium phosphate. It is given by INTRAMUSCULAR INJECTION and is REGISTERED AS A BOOSTER IN PEOPLE AGED 10 YEARS AND OVER
claims.source_text: Each 0.5 mL monodose vial or pre-filled syringe contains: ≥2 IU Diphtheria toxoid ≥20 IU Tetanus toxoid 2.5 µg Pertussis toxoid 5 µg Filamentous Haemagglutinin 3 µg Pertactin 5 µg Pertussis fimbriae types 2 and 3 … Administration route: Intramuscular injection … Registered as a booster in people aged ≥10 years.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Pertussis (whooping cough)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/pertussis-whooping-cough, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ NO ANTIBIOTIC, DOSE OR DURATION IS GIVEN for treatment or for post-exposure prophylaxis. The Handbook states antibiotic therapy is indicated if coryza started less than 21 days ago and refers to the CDNA national guidelines for pertussis, WHICH WERE NOT RETRIEVED. This compendium's `drug-choice-for-selected-infections` carries AMH's naming of azithromycin or clarithromycin, also WITHOUT A DOSE.
The CDNA (Communicable Diseases Network Australia) national guidelines for pertussis, named by the Handbook as the authority for management of cases and contacts, WERE NOT RETRIEVED.
